items.headline: UK unemployment falls to 4.6%, beating forecasts, but payrolls and job openings drop
items.caption: Britain's jobless rate dipped to 4.6% in the three months to September, lower than the 4.7% expected. Payrolls and vacancies both fell, so the job market is still cooling.

visual.title: UK jobless rate, 3 months to Sept
visual.foot: Lowest since early 2025, per ONS via Investing.com

detail: The UK's unemployment rate fell to 4.6% in the three months to September, the lowest since the period ending April 2025. Economists had expected 4.7%. The number of jobless people fell by 88,000 to about 1.68 million.
The details were weaker. The number of workers on company payrolls fell, vacancies dropped again, and regular pay growth slowed. Employers said higher labor and running costs are holding back hiring.
The statistics office said part of the drop came from changes in its survey sample, and the rate has a margin of error of 0.3 points. The next report is due December 15.
money: A cooler UK job market can ease wage-driven inflation, which matters for UK rates and the pound.
If you hold international stock funds, UK data like this can move British shares and the currency.
Planning a UK trip? Watch the pound; currency swings change what your dollars buy.
risk: Survey changes make the headline rate less reliable than usual.
Falling payrolls could point to more weakness ahead.

items.headline: Fed Chair Warsh lays out three ways 'superintelligence' could hit the economy
items.caption: At a Fed event in San Francisco, Warsh walked through a boom, a jobs-shock and a bust scenario for advanced AI. He said they are illustrations, not forecasts.

visual.title: Warsh's three AI scenarios
items: 1. Shared boom: workers and owners both gain
2. Fast growth, but jobs get displaced
3. AI returns disappoint and growth slows
Built by Fed staff models, not forecasts

detail: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh spoke Monday at a conference in San Francisco run by the Fed Board and the San Francisco Fed. It feeds a Fed task force studying how new technology affects jobs and productivity.

He outlined three paths. In the first, AI lifts productivity and gains are widely shared. In the second, growth speeds up but some jobs disappear and workers struggle to move. In the third, heavy AI spending and stock gains fail to pay off, and the economy slows.
Speakers included leaders from Stripe, Palo Alto Networks and Affirm. Warsh has said he wants to know if a productivity boom is coming fast or slowly, and what it means for jobs and prices.
money: Scenario 3 is a reminder: don't put too much of your portfolio in AI stocks alone.
Build skills that pair with AI tools; that can protect your income if jobs shift.
Keep an emergency fund; job shocks are easier to ride out with cash on hand.
risk: None of these paths is a Fed forecast.
AI views can shift rate expectations and move markets.

items.caption: CMS extended its nationwide freeze on new hospice and home health enrollments, citing fraud. Existing agencies keep serving patients and can now add locations.

detail: CMS said it will keep its nationwide moratorium on new Medicare hospice and home health agencies for six more months. The first freeze began May 13. Federal Register notices were set for November 16.
New agencies still can't enroll, and certain majority ownership changes are blocked. One change: agencies already enrolled can now add practice locations under their current enrollment.
CMS chief Mehmet Oz said fraud in these areas persists. In October, a two-day sweep in California led to 145 provider revocations tied to more than $703 million in Medicare and Medicaid payments.

items.headline: In 6 weeks, California starts charging sales tax on downloaded software and SaaS

detail: California will treat electronically delivered prewritten software, including software-as-a-service, as taxable starting Jan. 1, 2027. Gov. Newsom signed SB 122 on June 29.

detail: Treasury and the IRS created the IRA Compliance Resolution System (ICRS) under Revenue Procedure 2026-33. It opens May 1, 2027.

It covers four errors: missed required minimum distributions, IRA setup mistakes, errors by non-spouse heirs moving inherited money, and missed 60-day rollover deadlines. Regular filings before Jan. 1, 2028 cost $3,500.
A separate rule, Revenue Procedure 2026-34, widened the fix-it program for employer plans, including 403(b), SEP and SIMPLE IRA plans. Free automatic and self-certification options stay available.
money: Check now that you took this year's required IRA withdrawal; fixing it before Dec. 31 avoids needing any new program.
Moving money between accounts? Do a direct trustee-to-trustee transfer to avoid the 60-day rollover deadline.
If you inherited an IRA, review the payout rules with a pro; heir errors are among the most common.
risk: The $3,500 fee may cost more than some small errors; free self-correction may be better.

items.caption: Employers that laid off similar U.S. workers in the past two years could not file. Newspaper ads would give way to online recruiting.

visual.foot: Proposal only; current rules still apply.

detail: The Labor Department announced a proposed rule Monday to rewrite PERM, the labor-market test most employers must pass before sponsoring a worker for a job-based green card. Publication in the Federal Register was expected Nov. 17, starting a 60-day comment period.

money: Agents can compare prices for you; use them to find deals, but still check the final total before approving.
Temporary card numbers can reduce fraud risk if a store's data is hacked.
Set a budget before letting any app buy things for you, so small purchases don't add up.
risk: Mistakes by an AI agent could mean returns and disputes; know your card's dispute rights.
It is new, and rules on who is liable for agent errors are still forming.

Free open-weight models can cut AI costs for small businesses that can host them.
A broad tech fund spreads your bet across chip makers instead of one winner.

items.caption: The USS Theodore Roosevelt makes three US carriers in the Middle East for the first time since the Iraq war. Strikes and tanker attacks widened since Sunday.

items.t: Iran drones target US base in Bahrain
US hits launchers in southern Iran
IRGC claims 6 tankers on fire since Sunday

detail: The US and Iran traded wider strikes since Sunday. After an Iranian drone attack on a US base in Bahrain, the US hit Iranian missile launchers in Bandar Lengeh and Sirik, a wider area than before.
The USS Theodore Roosevelt joined two other carrier groups. It's the first time since the Iraq war that the US has three carriers in the region, with about 19 warships total.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard claims six tankers have caught fire since Sunday, which is unconfirmed. Iranian officials threatened US bases in Europe. Oil still fell Monday, with US crude near $84.
money: Gas prices are falling for now, but a wider war could reverse that fast; don't lock in big fuel-dependent plans on today's prices.
Energy and defense stocks often react to escalation; a broad fund avoids betting on headlines.
Keep an emergency fund; oil shocks can push up prices for many goods.
risk: A wider war could spike oil and shipping costs.
Reports from both sides are hard to verify quickly.

items.caption: Fewer than 20 ABC News staffers took early retirement, per reports. Disney is said to plan thousands more job cuts, likely in January.
detail: Several longtime ABC News senior staffers took Disney's voluntary early retirement offer. Most worked behind the scenes, and fewer than 20 ABC News people accepted, according to the New York Post.
The offer went to workers at least 50 years old with 10 or more years at Disney. Disney has cut jobs several times this year, including about 1,000 corporate roles in April.
Bloomberg reported Disney plans thousands more cuts, with some managers asked to target up to 20% in annual savings. Disney reports full-year results Tuesday at 8:30 a.m. ET.
money: If you're offered a buyout, compare it to severance you might get in a later layoff before deciding.
Check how a buyout affects your health coverage and retirement plan before signing.
Cost cuts can lift profits short term; watch Tuesday's guidance if you own Disney.

Diesel slipped to $5.999, under $6 for the first time since September. Its record was $6.52 on Sept. 22.

Use a gas app to compare stations; gaps of 30 cents or more a gallon are common.

items.headline: About 5 million have lost SNAP since the 2025 law; San Diego office now hands out food
items.caption: The drop is the fastest in decades and well above federal estimates. San Diego County has 36,000 fewer people on SNAP and is running free grocery events.
detail: About five million people have lost SNAP food benefits since the One Big Beautiful Bill passed in July 2025. The law cut funding, tightened eligibility and added new work rules.

In San Diego County, 36,000 fewer people were on SNAP in September than in July 2025. The county teamed up with food banks to hold free grocery giveaways outside social service offices, reaching over 5,200 people through September.
Elsewhere, Texas's application backlog grew from 3,700 in January to 175,000 in September. In Louisiana, three-quarters of removals came from paperwork issues like missed forms or interviews.
money: If you get SNAP, answer every notice and keep copies; many people lose benefits over missing paperwork.
Food banks and county grocery events can stretch a tight food budget; call 211 to find one.
If you were cut off, ask your county if you qualify for an exemption to the work rules.
risk: A new USDA proposal could remove millions more from SNAP.
Rules vary by state, so check with your local office.

detail: So-called neoclouds rent AI computing power built on Nvidia chips. They fell Monday as tech was the weakest sector, down about 2%, and money rotated out of AI and chip stocks.

The worry is funding. IREN's net debt jumped to about $4.43 billion from $216 million in one quarter, and it has a funding gap of roughly $6 billion. Nebius raised its 2026 spending plan to about $27 billion.
CoreWeave's revenue grew 168% to $3.66 billion last quarter, but its quarterly interest bill was $846 million. Nvidia's role in financing some of these build-outs is why its turmoil hits them.
money: Check if your tech fund holds these names; high-debt growth stocks can swing far more than the index.
Big backlogs are not cash; look at debt and interest costs before buying a fast grower.
If you want AI exposure with less risk, a broad index fund spreads it across many companies.

detail: J&J agreed to buy Ollin Biosciences for $2.2 billion upfront plus up to about $1.125 billion in milestones. The prize is OLN324, a Phase 3 drug for wet age-related macular degeneration and diabetic macular edema.
Blackstone will pay J&J $750 million over several years to fund the Phase 3 program, and gets milestone payments and single-digit royalties back. The deal should close before year-end.
Novartis and Sanofi also signed licensing deals Monday worth up to $2 billion and $1.2 billion.

Milestone payments are 'maybe' money; value deals on the upfront cash.

risk: Phase 3 drugs can still fail, as Monday's FDA rejection of another drug showed.

items.headline: DOJ final rule: immigrants have no constitutional right to an appeals board review
items.caption: The rule lets the Board of Immigration Appeals pick which cases to review and quickly dismiss others. DOJ cites a big backlog; advocates say it cuts due process.

visual.title: What the final rule does
items: Lets the appeals board quickly dismiss more cases
Says no constitutional right to a board appeal
10-day appeal deadline in lawyer discipline cases (was 30)
Ran as an interim rule earlier in 2026

detail: The Justice Department's immigration court office released a final rule Monday, due in the Federal Register the next day. It says there is no constitutional due process right to an administrative appeal before the Board of Immigration Appeals.
The rule gives board members wider discretion to choose cases and summarily dismiss others. It notes people can still challenge orders in federal court.
It took effect on an interim basis earlier this year. Advocates sued, saying it strips due process; DOJ says it is needed to cut a large backlog.
money: People in immigration court should confirm appeal deadlines with a qualified lawyer right away.
Nonprofit legal aid groups can lower the cost of representation.
Employers with immigrant staff may want to plan for faster case outcomes.
risk: Legal challenges to the rule may continue.

items.headline: Supreme Court will decide if Trump's border asylum ban went too far
items.caption: Lower courts said the president exceeded his authority by barring asylum claims from people who cross illegally. A ruling is expected by the end of June.
detail: The Supreme Court agreed Friday to hear the administration's appeal of rulings against its asylum restrictions at the southern border.
The policy, announced Jan. 20, 2025, bars people caught crossing illegally from seeking asylum and allows fast-track removals. It lasts until the president decides the 'invasion' has ended.
A DC judge ruled for immigrant groups in July 2025, and an appeals court agreed in April but largely paused its ruling so the case could go up. Arguments are expected in coming months.
money: Businesses relying on immigrant labor should plan for either outcome next summer.
Families with pending cases should keep documents current and seek legal advice.
Watch for scams promising asylum help; use accredited legal providers.
risk: The policy stays largely in place while the case is pending.
